[[File:Coriaria myrtifolia MHNT.BOT.2009.17.19.jpg|thumb|''Coriaria myrtifolia'' - [[MHNT]]]]

'''''Coriaria myrtifolia''''', called in English '''redoul''',  is a shrub that grows to 2–3 m tall. ''Myrtifolia'' means [[Myrtaceae|myrtle]]-like leaves.

The fruit is a fleshy black berry [[achene]] slightly similar to a [[blackberry]] but toxic. ''Coriaria myrtifolia'' has the largest fruits in the genus ''[[Coriaria]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|title= Pericarp anatomy and evolution inCoriaria (Coriariaceae) | doi=10.1007/BF02489422 | volume=105|issue=2|journal=The Botanical Magazine Tokyo|pages=289–302|year= 1992 |last1= Tobe |first1= Hiroshi |last2= Suzuki |first2= Mitsuo |last3= Fukuhara |first3= Tatsundo | s2cid=33868678 }}</ref> It is especially dangerous for children, who may eat it if they confuse it with edible berries. It should be recognized as one of the most neurotoxic plants in the western Mediterranean area.<ref name= Coriariamyrtifolia >{{cite journal |last= Pommier |first=  Philip |title=  Poisoning by Coriaria myrtifolia Linnaeus: A new case report and review of the literature|journal= Toxicon|date=November 2005 |volume= 46 |issue= 6 |pages= 600–603|doi=10.1016/j.toxicon.2005.06.026|pmid= 16165183 }}</ref>

==Range==
Geographically, this species is confined to northern Mediterranean coastal [[Spain]] and [[Southern France]] (from the [[Gironde]] to the [[Alpes Maritimes]]), penetrating into [[Italy]] as far as part of the [[Apennines]].  The species reappears in the western [[Rif]] and [[Algeria]], and in the [[Balearic Islands]] it appears only in [[Ibiza]].<ref name="MontserratNature">{{Cite journal |doi = 10.1038/182475a0|title = Root Nodules of Coriaria|journal = Nature|volume = 182|issue = 4633|pages = 475|year = 1958|last1 = Montserrat|first1 = Pedro|bibcode = 1958Natur.182..475M|s2cid = 4251802|doi-access = }}</ref> The oldest known mention of this plant, dating from 932, is in a place name and implies its presence in the County of [[Manresa]], north-west of [[Barcelona]].<ref>« In comitatum Manresa, in terminio de Kastro Rosetorium... », F. Udina Martorell, El Archivo condal de Barcelona en los siglos ix-x. Estudio crítico de sus fondos, Barcelona, 1951, p. 204, § 104.</ref>

In all this range, this plant plays an important role in preventing soil erosion and serves as understory vegetation. It is extraordinarily abundant in the less dense woodlands of the Spanish provinces of [[Province of Girona|Girona]] and [[Province of Barcelona|Barcelona]] (eastern part) at altitudes of 200–600 m, reaching occasionally to 1,000 m.<ref name="MontserratNature" />

==Name==
The [[Spanish language|Spanish]] name ''emborrachacabras'' (i.e. ''makes goats drunk'') refers to the leaves' intoxicating effect on goats that eat them. The [[French language|French]] name is ''Corroyère à feuilles de myrte''. The [[Occitan language|Occitan]] name (''rodor'') and [[Catalan language|Catalan]] name (''roldor'') derive from [[Latin]] ''Rhus tyrius'' (''[[Rhus coriaria]]''), referring to the leaves' use in the traditional [[Tanning (leather)|tannery]] industry. In Morocco, it's called ''arwaz'' (أرواز) in [[Berber languages|Berber]] as well as the spoken [[Moroccan Arabic]].<ref name="chafik">{{Cite book|title=الدارجة المغربية، مجال توارد بين الأمازيغية و العربية|author=Mohamed Chafik|page=45}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Coriaria myrtifolia - Flor roldor.jpg|thumb|left|A flowering plant ([[Castelltallat]])]]The root nodules of this plant carry out symbiotic [[nitrogen fixation]],<ref>{{cite journal|title= Fixation of Nitrogen in Coriaria myrtifolia | volume=193 | issue=4820|doi=10.1038/1931103a0|journal=Nature|pages=1103–1104|year= 1962 |last1= Bond |first1= G. | bibcode=1962Natur.193.1103B | s2cid=4158931 }}</ref> ''Coriaria myrtifolia'' is one of the 13 ''[[Coriaria]]'' species known to bear [[Actinorhizal plant|actinorhizae]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://md1.csa.com/partners/viewrecord.php?requester=gs&collection=ENV&recid=1925382&q=Coriaria+myrtifolia&uid=790317218&setcookie=yes |title=CSA |access-date=2011-01-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120404174847/http://md1.csa.com/partners/viewrecord.php?requester=gs&collection=ENV&recid=1925382&q=Coriaria+myrtifolia&uid=790317218&setcookie=yes |archive-date=2012-04-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The redoul is a shrub with branches greyish square section. The leaves are sessile, mostly opposite but sometimes in groups of three or more, oblong, acuminate, with three ribs. The small greenish flowers, which appear from April to June in racemes, have five reddish highlights styles, five sepals and five petals, with ten stamens. The black fruits are formed of five fleshy carpels, each containing one seed.

==Toxicity==
The leaves and fruits of ''Coriaria myrtifolia'' contain coriamyrtin, a typical convulsant substance<ref name= CORIAMYRTIN >{{cite journal |last= E. SWANSON |first= EDWARD |title=pharmacology |journal= The Pharmacological Action of Coriamyrtin|date=August 1936 |volume= 57 |issue= 4 |pages=  410–418 |url= http://jpet.aspetjournals.org/content/57/4/410.abstract |accessdate= 19 September 2013 |url-access= <!--WP:URLACCESS--> }}</ref> one member of {{chem name|picrotoxane}} [[sesquiterpenes]], was first isolated in 1864.<ref name= coriamyrtin >{{cite journal |last= Tanaka |first=  Kiyoshi |date=September 1982 |volume= 57 |issue= 4 |pages=  410–418 |doi=10.1021/ja00382a047|title= Stereocontrolled total synthesis of (.+-.)-coriamyrtin |journal= Journal of the American Chemical Society }}</ref>

Toxic effects are characterized by digestive ([[nausea]], [[vomiting]], [[abdominal pain]]), neurological (obnubilation, convulsions and their complications), and respiratory disorders (polypnea, respiratory problems, [[apnea]], short and superficial respiration) together with [[myositis]] of the pupils. Treatment of this poisoning is purely symptomatic. In the case of convulsions, rapid [[resuscitation]] in an intensive care unit is necessary. Coriamyrtin also has a pharmacological action.<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=12422481 | volume=31 | issue=33 | title=[Acute intoxication by redoul (Coriaria myrtifolia L.). Three observations] |date=October 2002 | journal=Presse Med | pages=1554–6 | last1 = Skalli | first1 = S | last2 = David | first2 = JM | last3 = Benkirane | first3 = R | last4 = Zaid | first4 = A | last5 = Soulaymani | first5 = R}}</ref>

The [[Honeydew (secretion)|honeydew]] from redoul is also toxic.<ref name= PalynologicalObservations1950 >{{Cite journal |doi = 10.2307/2482183|jstor = 2482183|title = Palynological Observations on Some Spanish Honeys|journal = Bulletin of the Torrey Botanical Club|volume = 77|issue = 6|pages = 495–502|year = 1950|last1 = Vieitez|first1 = Ernesto}}</ref>

==Uses==
Traditionally, leaves of redoul were intensively collected for their [[tannin]] content, for tanning and dyeing purposes.
During the medieval period, ecclesiastical institutions and the aristocracy clearly sought to establish some royalties on this resource, the samples are being especially on the distribution and sale of material first. These uses are due to the wealth of ''Coriaria spp'' tannin, particularly concentrated in the root and the bark of the stem, but also present in leaves, where they coexist with yellow dyes from the chemical group of [[flavonoids]]. These tannins are part of the group of hydrolyzable tannins, such as [[gall]] tannins. The chemical composition of redoul thus makes a tanning substance, capable of transforming recently flayed animal skins into leather, which is rot resistant, flexible and relatively impermeable, known as Basil leather.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.basane.fr/en/history2.php|title=Basane.fr - Basil - History}}</ref>  These properties allow for its widespread use in many industries. Moreover, the well-known chemical reaction of tannins with iron salts, producing black precipitates, is the basis for the manufacture of some [[ink]]s used since the Middle Ages, and is also used to dye a variety of textiles black or gray. Until the mid-fourteenth century, the material was the subject of extensive trade between the north of [[Catalonia]] and [[Languedoc]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=  http://medievales.revues.org/3443?&id=3443|title=  Le redoul, herbe des tanneurs et des teinturiers. Collecte, commercialisation et utilisations d'une plante sauvage dans l'espace méridional (xiiie-xve siècles) |journal= Médiévales. Langues, Textes, Histoire |date= December 2007 |issue= 53 |pages= 51–64 |doi= 10.4000/medievales.3443 |last1= Cardon |first1= Dominique |last2= Pinto |first2= Anthony |doi-access= free }}</ref> The [[Māori people|Māori]] used species of ''[[Coriaria]]'' from New Zealand: they produced traditional tattoo inks from the fruit juice, made musical instruments from the hollow stems, and despite its extreme toxicity ate the fruit sparingly due to its sweet taste; using it to sweeten drinking water or jellies made from seaweed.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics vol. 2|author=Wilson & Wilkins|year=1911}}</ref>

''Coriaria myrtifolia'' is also used as an [[ornamental plant]].<ref>{{cite web|url=  http://www.mapa.es/ministerio/pags/biblioteca/revistas/pdf_hortint/hortint_2004_46_62_67.pdf |title=  El sector de la planta ornamental en la Península Ibérica}}</ref>
